The three steps by which Russia, Prussia and Austria divided the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth between them, in 1772, 1793 and 1795, wiping it off the map for 123 years.

The Commonwealth was large but weak. Its kings were elected, and any noble in its parliament could block a law. Its neighbours, above all Catherine the Great of Russia, kept it that way with bribes and troops.

  • 1772: Russia, Prussia and Austria each took a slice of border land.
  • 1793: The Poles tried to reform. The Constitution of 3 May 1791, one of the first written constitutions in Europe, strengthened the state. Russia invaded, and Russia and Prussia took a second, larger share.
  • 1795: Tadeusz Kościuszko led a rising in 1794, which was crushed. The three powers divided the rest.

The Polish nation lived on without a state. Polish soldiers fought for Napoleon, who set up a small Duchy of Warsaw, and Poles rose against Russia in 1830 and 1863. Poland came back as an independent state only in 1918.
sum: The three steps by which Russia, Prussia and Austria divided the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth between them, in 1772, 1793 and 1795, wiping it off the map for 123 years.
